newsitem.title: JAPAN: Algeria crude output seen above 1 mln bpd by 2000.
newsitem.headline: Algeria crude output seen above 1 mln bpd by 2000.

text.p: Production of Algerian crude will increase to more than one million barrels per day (bpd) by 2000 from current levels of about 750,000 bpd, an official from Algeria's state oil company told a symposium on Wednesday.

Ahmed Khodja Abdelmadjid, director of the crude condensate and products marketing division at Sonatrach, said Algeria's crude production would increase in line with a rise in partnerships with foreign companies.
"Production of crude with foreign companies will reach 32 percent (of total output) in year 2000 from 9.7 percent in 1996," he said.
He was speaking at a symposium in Tokyo on modernisation of the petroleum industry attended by oil industry officials from 18 countries.
Algiers passed legislation in 1991 permitting foreign licensees.
"By the year 2000, 15 to 20 percent of the crude oil production will be marketed by our partners," Abdelmadjid said.
During 1996, crude exports of 50,000 bpd by Italy's Agip SpA account for about six percent of Algerian crude exports, he said.

From September this year, three other partners, Petro-Canada, Spain's Cia Espanola de Petroleos SA and U.S. firm Atlantic Richfield Co, would lift and market crude under production-sharing contracts, Abdelmadjid said.
U.S. firm Anadarko Petroleum Corp would begin exporting Algerian crude from the Hassi Berkine field in 1998, he said.
Marketing of Algerian crude was dominated by Sonatrach until October 1995, he said.

Condensate output would be maintained at 1996 levels of 16 million tonnes with falling output from the Hassi R'Mel field compensated by development of new fields, such as the Hamra and Tin Fouye TabanKort fields, Abdelmadjid said.

He said production of natural gas would grow to 134 billion cubic metres in 2000 from 113 billion cubic metres in 1995, while production of liquefied natural gas would double to 9.6 million tonnes in the same period.
The total output of hydrocarbons in 2000 would be more than 200 million tonnes-oil-equivalent, four times the level of production in 1971, Abdelmadjid said.
To sustain growth in output, an overall investment of $18 billion would be needed, he said.
